lines: A colleague tells you Gorilla's encoder will shrink this plant's storage bill by a factor of twelve.
Two weeks later, measured on this plant's own readings, the real reduction is barely better than one.
Nothing is broken. The same algorithm, the same code, just a different kind of data underneath it.
Gorilla's first trick is on the timestamps: instead of storing each one, it stores how much the gap between readings changed from the gap before it.
Its second trick is on the values: it compares each float's bit pattern against the one before it using exclusive-or, which leaves mostly zeros when the two are close.
Reproduce the paper's own two worked examples by hand, bit for bit, and they land exactly where the paper says they land.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal answers it.
Run that exact same encoder on a signal that changes constantly and carries far more precision than the one Gorilla was built around.
Does it still compress nearly as well?
answer: Both tricks only pay off when successive readings stay close together — a signal that jumps around with no pattern breaks that assumption completely.

lines: Put three very different signals through the identical, unmodified encoder.
On a slow, barely-changing signal, it shrinks the data by a huge amount.
On a noisy, high-precision signal, the very same code barely helps at all. The ratio was never a property of the algorithm alone.
A later refinement called Chimp notices that a short run of trailing zeros isn't worth spending bits to describe separately, so below a certain length it just keeps them.
A further version compares each new reading against many earlier readings instead of only the one right before it.
That wider comparison wins specifically when a signal keeps repeating a pattern it saw a while ago.
A sensor reporting a reading with two decimal places is storing a floating-point number whose very lowest bits are really just measurement noise.
A newer codec treats that same reading as a small, exact whole number instead, with no bit-pattern guessing involved at all.
This is the approach one popular embedded database actually uses as its own default choice for floating-point columns.
Separately from the readings themselves, every row also carries a label: which piece of equipment, which signal.
Those labels repeat across an enormous number of rows, drawn from a tiny set of distinct strings.

A lookup table for the distinct strings, plus counting how many times each one repeats in a row, collapses that column to almost nothing — so whatever size is left over belongs almost entirely to the readings themselves.
Timestamps that change gently and values that barely move favor the first two tricks this topic covered.
A signal that keeps repeating a pattern favors comparing against many earlier readings instead of just one.

A signal that's fundamentally decimal favors treating it as an exact small integer instead of guessing at its bit pattern — and a lossy option exists too, but only if it states exactly how far it's allowed to drift.
One more case worth reasoning through before moving on.
A vendor claims their compression codec beats every other codec, on every kind of workload, without exception.
Given everything just measured across three different signals, should a claim like that survive contact with this plant's own readings?
answer: Every single codec measured here won clearly on one kind of signal and lost clearly on another — a compression ratio is a claim about the shape of the data, never a universal ranking of one codec over all the rest.
